strengths: Novel integration of neural ODEs with causal graph discovery for GRNs, enabling simultaneous trajectory inference and network inference from large-scale perturbation data.
Biologically motivated architecture: gene modules, Hill-like sigmoid activation, decay term, and explicit shift interventions for over-expression and perfect interventions.

Demonstrated scalability to thousands of genes and hundreds of interventions on the TF Atlas dataset, outperforming scalable baselines (NO-TEARS, DCDFG) in recall and p-value, and competitive with DCDI on smaller simulated datasets.
Includes interpretability analysis of inferred gene modules with gene set enrichment and stability/generalizability assessments, showing biological relevance.
Well-structured presentation with extensive appendix detailing hyperparameters, simulation setup, and additional results.
weaknesses: GRN inference precision is very low (e.g., 0.0046 on yeast, ~0.004 on TF Atlas), meaning the vast majority of predicted edges are false positives, which limits practical utility despite high recall and significant p-values.

Evaluation on real data is one-sided (recall and p-value only) because ground truth contains only positive edges; precision and false discovery rate are not reported, making it hard to assess overall network quality relative to baselines.

Threshold selection for binarizing the inferred GRN is heuristic and may favor higher recall; baselines use different thresholding procedures, raising fairness concerns, though the paper partially addresses this with sparsity-vs-recall curves.

Held-out intervention prediction shows high variance and fails on several TFs (SETDB1, POU2AF1, TEAD1 with W2 > 240 vs. baseline ~100), contradicting the claim of robust generalization; no analysis of these failures is provided.
Theoretical identifiability is only conjectured for the ODE case, relying on an unpublished SDE result; no rigorous proof or clear conditions are given.

The extracted GRN matrix G = A diag(α) B ignores the state-dependent derivative of the sigmoid activation, so the effective interaction strengths are misrepresented; this may affect edge sign and magnitude interpretation.
Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or data release statement for PerturbODE itself, though hyperparameters and baseline code are referenced.
Limitations are only briefly mentioned in the discussion and conclusion; no dedicated limitations section addresses the precision issues or the model's assumptions.

strengths: Novel and elegant integration of a biologically structured neural ODE with optimal-transport (Wasserstein-2) training and explicit intervention terms; the factorization G = A diag(α)B reduces the parameter count from d² to 2dl, which enables scaling to 817 genes and ~1000+ perturbations where DCDI and Bicycle cannot run.

Biologically motivated design choices are reasonable: sigmoid activation justified via its relationship to the Hill function, a strictly positive decay term for stability, an explicit intervention/shift term, and a masking matrix for perfect interventions. The gene-module interpretation is supported by GSEA showing enrichment for relevant developmental pathways (anterior-posterior axis, vascular endothelium) with p < 0.001 against random matrices.

Held-out intervention prediction is the most convincing result: Pearson r = 0.67 vs. ~0 for the linear SCM baselines, and lower W2 for 7 of 10 held-out TFs, which is a genuinely nontrivial generalization result.
Clear positioning relative to prior work (NO-TEARS, DCDI, DCDFG, Bicycle, neural-ODE trajectory methods) and a well-organized presentation of the framework.
weaknesses: The core GRN-discovery claim is barely supported by the evidence. On the yeast SERGIO benchmark, PerturbODE's precision is 0.0046 and AUPRC is 0.0044 (Table 4) while the ground-truth edge density is ~0.0039 (623 edges over 400×399 possible). This is essentially at random-chance level. The method predicts 43,655 edges for a 623-edge network (Table 3), meaning almost all predictions are false positives. Statistical significance against Erdős-Rényi random graphs is an extremely weak standard — any method that predicts many edges will beat random — yet it is used as the central evidence of GRN-recovery quality.

The claimed superiority is contradicted by the reported numbers. On the 400-gene yeast dataset and the 100-gene random DAGs, DCDI matches or beats PerturbODE (better AUPRC, F1, and p-value in Table 4, and the text concedes DCDI performs better on random DAGs). The advantage emerges only in regimes where DCDI cannot run, so the evidence does not support a general claim of better GRN inference.

TF Atlas GRN evaluation reports only recall and p-value because the ground truth contains only positive edges, and does not quantify false discoveries. With ~101,404 predicted edges (~15% density) in the 817-gene network and recall of ~0.36–0.50, the false-positive rate is unaddressed, making the GRN claim uninterpretable.

Held-out intervention results are reported selectively. The text states PerturbODE makes 'considerably better predictions for the vast majority,' but it is substantially worse than NO-TEARS-LR for 3 of 10 held-out TFs (SETDB1 262 vs 97, POU2AF1 301 vs 105, TEAD1 245 vs 106), and the aggregate W2 is 84 ± 183 — a standard deviation larger than the mean, indicating severe instability that is not discussed.

The 'trajectory inference' contribution is not validated. Only day-0 control and day-7 endpoints are available; the ODE path between them is entirely unconstrained, and no intermediate time points are used to validate the inferred trajectories, so the dynamical modeling claim rests on endpoint matching alone.

Parameter identifiability — a point the authors themselves flag as delicate (Section 5) and on which the parameter-recovery claim ultimately depends — is deferred to a placeholder reference ('Authors (2025)') that is not a properly identified citation. This is a serious evidential and presentation gap for the paper's central theoretical assumption.

Thresholding is arbitrary and inconsistent: c is chosen 'for clarity of presentation by getting similar number of edges as DCDI' (Appendix A.2.1), and the baselines are compared at fixed author-recommended thresholds at which NO-TEARS/NO-TEARS-LR produce near-empty graphs (0 edges for yeast). This makes the baseline comparison potentially unfair and the sparsity-versus-recall curves hard to interpret.

The diffusion-based regularization (Section 3.4), introduced with a claim of establishing equivalence to a deterministic SCM via the Contraction Mapping Theorem, is never ablated, so its contribution is unquantified. Similarly, the claim that the model handles regulatory cycles is not demonstrated empirically.

Reproducibility is limited: no code, data-processing scripts, or artifact release is mentioned, and key hyperparameters and threshold choices appear hand-tuned per dataset in ways that are hard to reconstruct.

strengths: The paper proposes a novel and biologically motivated neural ODE framework that factorizes a gene regulatory network into low-rank module structure (G = A diag(alpha) B), enabling scalable GRN inference while explicitly modeling perturbation shifts and decay.

It addresses an important and timely problem: causal/regulatory network discovery from large-scale single-cell perturbation data such as the TF Atlas, where many existing causal graph methods cannot scale.

The method is evaluated on both SERGIO simulations and the real TF Atlas dataset, and the held-out intervention prediction results (e.g., Pearson r = 0.67 vs near-zero for linear SCMs) are promising if correct.

The model provides a degree of interpretability through inferred gene modules, and the reported module-level analyses align with known developmental GRNs and pathways, with p-values against random graphs.

The paper includes substantial implementation details, hyperparameters, and some limitations discussion, including the delicate nature of identifiability and the limitations of positive-only ground-truth edges.
weaknesses: The central claim of deriving a causal GRN is not rigorously supported: identifiability is only discussed informally and deferred to an anonymous/unpublished reference for a low-noise SDE extension, with no proof for the noiseless ODE case used here.

The real-data GRN evaluation is limited by ground truth containing only positive edges, so precision and false-positive rates are not evaluated. With over 100,000 predicted edges on 817 genes, recall-only and p-value comparisons against random graphs can be inflated by dense predictions; overprediction is acknowledged but not adequately controlled.

Baselines on the large real TF Atlas are weak: DCDI and Bicycle cannot scale, so the strongest comparisons are against NO-TEARS variants with near-zero recall. On SERGIO simulations, DCDI matches or exceeds PerturbODE in low-dimensional settings, making the main practical advantage scalability rather than superior inference accuracy.

Held-out intervention prediction is inconsistent: for SETDB1, POU2AF1, and TEAD1, PerturbODE's W2 distance is much worse than NO-TEARS-LR despite the average advantage. Table 1 reports PerturbODE W2 = 84 +/- 183, which appears inconsistent with the individual W2 values in Table 2 and raises concerns about the summary statistics.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no PerturbODE code or environment is released; threshold selection is partly post hoc (chosen to yield 'reasonable' edge counts or match DCDI); the number of interventions and computational scaling are not clearly reported; and p-value/module-selection analyses lack multiple-testing correction.

The interpretability evidence is potentially post hoc: the seven modules are selected from 200 as the highest scoring, then tested for enrichment, with pathways filtered to relevant developmental categories. This can overstate biological discovery without correction for selection or multiple comparisons.

Presentation quality is uneven: reference errors/placeholders (e.g., 'Authors (2025)', inconsistent years, typo 'Olshtein-Uhlenbeck'), low-quality figures, and some duplicated tables make the manuscript harder to evaluate.

Scalability claims are not quantitatively benchmarked: the largest experiment is 817 genes, not thousands, and there is no runtime, memory, or convergence scaling analysis to justify large-scale causal discovery claims.

strengths: The paper proposes a novel and timely combination of neural ODEs, low-rank gene-module factorization, and interventional shifts for GRN discovery and trajectory prediction from perturbation scRNA-seq data.

It addresses real scalability limitations: the method is demonstrated on the TF Atlas dataset with 812 genes and thousands of perturbations, whereas several causal discovery baselines fail due to memory or numerical instability.

The model is interpretable: extracting G = A diag(alpha) B from the ODE parameters and analyzing latent modules recovers biologically plausible developmental GRNs, supported by GSEA and module-level analyses.
The framework can handle both perfect and imperfect interventions, including overexpression and knockout, and can model nonlinearity and cycles, unlike standard DAG-based SCMs.

The paper includes detailed preprocessing, hyperparameters, compute resources, ablation/power analyses, stability/generalizability checks, and a broader impacts statement, which improves transparency.

The Discussion and Conclusion appropriately acknowledge identifiability concerns and limitations rather than hiding them; the biological validation via TF Atlas and ChIP-Atlas adds practical relevance.
weaknesses: The central causal discovery claim is not established. There is no identifiability proof or consistency argument for recovering the true GRN from the neural ODE parameters; the Discussion defers this to anonymous future work. In particular, the extracted matrix G = A diag(alpha) B ignores the state-dependent sigmoid derivative and the decay term, so it is not the true Jacobian/causal effect and may assign edges where actual instantaneous effects are negligible.

Empirical GRN recovery on simulations is weak. Reported AUPRC values are often near random-chance levels (e.g., PerturbODE 0.0521 on 100-gene random DAGs, where the base positive rate is about 0.05), and PerturbODE is frequently outperformed by GENIE3, DCDI, or NO-TEARS. On the yeast 400-gene simulation, DCDI achieves higher AUPRC. Thus the results do not convincingly support robust GRN discovery.

On the real TF Atlas benchmark, evaluation uses positive-only reference networks and reports recall/p-values, not precision, F1, or AUROC. The ChIP-Atlas table shows FDR around 50% across thresholds, meaning about half of predicted edges are false discoveries. This severely limits the practical utility of the inferred networks.

The statistical significance tests compare against Erdos-Renyi random graphs with the same density, which only shows that predictions are non-random, not that they are causally correct or competitive. More rigorous false discovery control and calibration analyses are needed.

Threshold selection is partly tuned to match ground-truth edge counts in simulations and to make GENIE3/PerturbODE predict similar numbers of edges on TF Atlas, which risks optimistic or non-neutral comparisons across methods.

Held-out intervention prediction is not convincing. PerturbODE is worse than GEARS in W2 distance (median 84 vs 65) and has high variance and catastrophic errors for some transcription factors (e.g., SETDB1, POU2AF1, TEAD1). The claim that it is competitive relies on beating linear/scGPT baselines, not on matching the strongest available predictor.

The scalability advantage is partly demonstrated by excluding Bicycle and DCDI due to resource constraints, while DCDI outperforms PerturbODE where it can run. This makes it difficult to conclude that PerturbODE dominates existing methods rather than merely being more scalable.

Presentation and reproducibility have issues: several references and typos are erroneous (e.g., anonymous "Autthors [2025]", inconsistent years), figure/text ordering is confusing in places, and no code release is mentioned for PerturbODE itself. The method is described in enough detail to be approximated, but full reproducibility would benefit from released code and data splits.

strengths: Introduces a novel and biologically motivated neural-ODE framework that factorizes gene-gene regulation through low-dimensional modules, deriving a GRN estimate from A diag(alpha) B.

Addresses an important scalability problem in causal GRN discovery: it can train on a real 812-gene TF Atlas dataset with many overexpression interventions, whereas Bicycle and DCDI fail or are excluded due to memory/numerical issues.

Combines interventional modeling, optimal-transport distribution matching, and interpretable module extraction, with a promising qualitative analysis of inferred modules via GSEA and known developmental GRNs.
Evaluates on real TF Atlas data and includes held-out intervention prediction experiments with UMAP and cell-type-distance comparisons against GEARS, scGPT, and linear SCM baselines.
Provides extensive appendix details on simulations, hyperparameters, preprocessing, stability/generalizability analysis, and broader impacts, which are useful for follow-up work.
The application to TF overexpression and directed differentiation is timely and biologically relevant, and the idea of using ODE parameters for causal graph discovery is original.
weaknesses: The central causal-identifiability claim is not established. The paper admits that it relies on a cited unpublished 2025 result for a low-noise SDE extension and only conjectures identifiability for the noiseless ODE case when interventions exceed gene dimension. Without a proof or clear conditions, the extracted GRN cannot be reliably interpreted as a causal graph.

The inferred GRN matrix G = A diag(alpha) B omits the nonlinear saturation and decay terms. The actual local gene-gene interaction (Jacobian) is A diag(alpha sigma'(z)) B - W, so G may not represent direct causal regulatory effects and may be distorted by module activation and RNA decay.

The paper claims to model cellular differentiation trajectories, but it trains only from control initial states to 7-day endpoints; there are no intermediate time-course measurements or validation that the inferred ODE trajectories correspond to real biological dynamics. Thus the trajectory claim is largely unsupported.

The empirical GRN-inference results do not support the claimed superiority. On BoolODE 10-gene data, PerturbODE performs worse than NO-TEARS and GENIE3; on SERGIO 100-gene data, DCDI and GENIE3 marginally outperform it; on the 400-gene yeast network, DCDI achieves the highest performance. The conclusion that PerturbODE outperforms existing scalable methods on SERGIO-simulated data is misleading.

Real-data GRN evaluation is weak: the three TF Atlas human reference GRNs contain only positive edges, so only recall and p-values are reported. High recall can be obtained by predicting very dense graphs; Table 3 reports 101,404 predicted edges for 812 genes, and Table 1 shows FDR around 50-55%, not clearly better than GENIE3 at low thresholds.

Held-out intervention prediction is not convincingly specified or superior. It is unclear how the intervention strength s_j for an unseen TF is chosen without its perturbation data. GEARS achieves better W2 distance (65 vs 84), and PerturbODE's W2 has enormous variance (84 +/- 88) due to large mispredictions such as POU2AF1 (300.8) and SETDB1 (261.9).

Statistical evaluation is insufficient. P-values are computed against random graphs but not per edge, and there are no significance tests for predictive-performance comparisons across only 10 held-out TFs. Threshold choices (c, lambda, number of modules) appear tuned in ways that may advantage PerturbODE, while baselines use their own thresholds.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release for PerturbODE is mentioned, details of the held-out intervention setup and s_j inference are missing, and the key identifiability citation is anonymous/unverifiable.

Presentation contains inconsistencies and typos, e.g., the abstract/conclusion overstate performance relative to the figures and tables, and several claims (such as outperforming all linear methods or achieving the highest AUPRC) need clearer qualification. This makes the contribution hard to assess.

The limitations discussion is too narrow. It focuses on identifiability but omits the weak real-data FDR, lack of time-resolved trajectory validation, performance relative to simple baselines, computational cost, and the gap between the method's claims and empirical evidence.

strengths: The paper proposes a novel and useful integration of interpretable neural ODEs with intervention modeling for gene regulatory network discovery and perturbation response prediction, scaling to 812 genes on the TF Atlas dataset.

The method explicitly encodes perturbations via shift and perfect-intervention masking, uses distribution-level Wasserstein matching, and can predict unseen interventions, which is a meaningful capability over standard causal graph discovery methods.

The module-based parameterization A diag(alpha) B provides a degree of interpretability: inferred modules are analyzed with GSEA and linked to known developmental pathways such as anterior-posterior axis specification, trophoblast induction, and angiogenesis.

Empirical results on the TF Atlas are promising: PerturbODE achieves the highest recall and ChIP-Atlas AUPRC among the compared scalable methods, with improved statistical significance, and its held-out perturbation predictions beat linear SCMs and scGPT on W2 and cell-type distance while being competitive with GEARS.
Scalability is convincingly better than DCDI, DCDFG, and Bicycle on large real data, where the baselines either fail numerically or run out of memory.

The appendix is extensive, covering preprocessing, hyperparameters, simulator extensions, ablation studies, stability analysis, compute resources, and broader impacts, which supports reproducibility in principle.
weaknesses: The central causal-discovery claim is not rigorously established. The extracted graph G = A diag(alpha) B ignores the state-dependent sigmoid derivative and decay term, so it is not the Jacobian or a direct causal effect matrix; identifiability is only discussed informally and deferred to future work. This weakens the claim that the neural ODE parameters recover a causal GRN.

Real-data GRN evaluation shows high false discovery rates around 50-55% at multiple thresholds, and some TF Atlas references contain only positive edges, so only recall is reported. The AUPRC values on ChIP-Atlas are very small, and it is unclear whether the inferred edges are causal or simply predictive associations.

Benchmark performance is mixed: on BoolODE, 100-gene SERGIO, and yeast SERGIO, PerturbODE is comparable to or worse than methods such as DCDI, GENIE3, NO-TEARS, and Bicycle. The advantages appear mainly at large scale, so the conclusion that it outperforms scalable methods on SERGIO-simulated data is overstated.

Held-out intervention prediction is weaker than GEARS in W2 distance and has very large variance for some TFs, with individual errors above 240 for SETDB1, POU2AF1, and TEAD1. The paper does not analyze these failure cases, and it is unclear how the intervention strength s is determined for unseen perturbations.

Key reproducibility details are missing or ambiguous: no code release is mentioned, threshold selection is heuristic and sometimes tuned to match baseline edge counts, and the reported numbers of predicted edges are difficult to reconcile across Table 1 and Table 3. The optional diffusion regularization is not ablated, so its contribution is not demonstrated.

The module interpretation analysis is post-hoc and based on selected top modules; multiple comparisons and selection bias are not fully addressed. This makes the biological interpretability claims suggestive rather than conclusive.

Several methodological choices are under-justified: L1 is applied only to B rather than the final GRN G, final graph sparsity depends on arbitrary thresholding, and the Sinkhorn approximation is treated as W2 without detailed error analysis. Presentation also has minor inconsistencies and typos in references.
